results.result: The manuscript reports that approximately 230 K99 awards were made annually from 2006-2021, representing up to $250 million in annual investment. From 2008-2021, there were an average of 234 extramural K99 awards per year, and from 2009-2022, an average of 198 R00 awards per year.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C2, C52, C57, and C58 provide consistent descriptive statistics about K99 and R00 award numbers based on NIH Reporter data. The values are internally consistent (e.g., ~230 vs 234 average awards) and represent straightforward data summaries with no complex statistical analysis required.

results.result: The manuscript demonstrates that approximately 89% of K99 awardees received R00 funding on a rolling yearly basis, with 78% overall conversion (2701 of 3456 extramural K99 awardees). The rolling conversion rate excluding 2006-2007 was 81.8%. Starting in 2015, R00 activation rates diverged between those staying at the same institution (69.4% average) versus moving to different institutions (93.9% average).
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C37, C59-C68 present conversion rate data with clear denominators and numerators. The temporal trend showing divergence starting in 2015 is supported by Figure 1C. The calculations are straightforward proportions that can be verified from the raw data described.

results.result: The manuscript reports that about 40% of K99 awardees were women (58% men), with the same conversion rates to R00 awards for both genders. Men have received more K99 awards than women each year since 2006, though the percentage of women receiving K99 awards has risen slightly in the most recent decade.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C99-C103 rely on name-to-gender classification using GenderAPI, which the authors acknowledge is 'inherently biased unevenly across demographics and groups' (C200). The methodology cannot capture transgender, non-binary, or gender non-conforming individuals, and may misclassify names. While the data show trends, the fundamental measurement approach introduces systematic uncertainty.

results.result: Institutions with the most NIH funding produced the most K99 awardees and recruited the most R00 awardees. K99 awards were granted to 256 institutions while R00 awardees represented 357 institutions. K99 awards were highly concentrated: 54% of awardees were at 10% of institutions, with Stanford alone having 237 K99 awardees. R00 awards were more geographically dispersed, with 73% of K99 awards on East/West coasts versus 55% of R00 awards.
results.evaluation: Claims C5-C6 and C72-C85 present descriptive statistics about institutional concentration supported by Figure 2 and the underlying NIH Reporter data. The geographic concentration metrics and specific institutional counts are straightforward data summaries. The claim that institutions with most NIH funding produce and recruit the most awardees is directly supported by Figure 3 and the data analysis.

results.result: Most K99 awardees (62%) attained faculty positions at private institutions. Private institutions with highest NIH funding hired R00 faculty primarily from other private institutions (31.2% top-funded, 46.9% lower-funded). Public institutions with smaller NIH portfolios hired 74% of K99 awardees from similar institutions. Self-hiring rates varied by institution type: 36% at top-funded private, 30.9% at top-funded public, 23.3% at lower-funded private, and 18.5% at lower-funded public institutions.
results.evaluation: Claims C86-C98 present hiring flow patterns supported by Table 1 and Figure 3. The percentages are calculated from the matched K99-R00 dataset (n=2703). The institutional classification into public/private and top-25/lower-funded is clearly defined in Methods. The self-hiring rates and cross-institutional hiring patterns are straightforward proportions from the data.

results.result: K99 awards were concentrated at top-funded institutions: 45% of K99 awards went to the top 25 highest funded institutions (representing only 24 institutions), while 55% went to 226 lower-funded institutions. R00 awards were more evenly distributed: 32% to top 25 institutions and 68% to 327 lower-funded institutions. Top-25 institutions averaged 65.5 K99 and 38.2 R00 awards per institution, versus 8.4 K99 and 5.8 R00 awards for lower-funded institutions.
results.evaluation: Claims C104-C112 present institutional concentration metrics supported by Figure 5 and Tables 3-4. The classification of institutions into top-25 versus lower-funded is clearly defined in Methods based on 2022 NIH funding levels. The percentages and averages are straightforward calculations from the data.

results.result: Time from R00 start to major NIH award (R01/DP2/R35) ranged from 4.6 to 7.4 years. Cox proportional hazard modeling identified three significant factors affecting future funding: staying at same institution (HR=0.7095, p<0.0001), R00 institution not in top-25 NIH funding (p<0.0001), and being a woman (p=0.001). Each cumulative disadvantage increased median time by ~6 months and reduced overall chance by 5-6%. Men moving to top-funded institutions had shortest time (4.6 years, 84.6% chance), while women staying at lower-funded institutions had longest time (7.4 years, 60% chance).
results.evaluation: Claims C7-C10 and C113-C123 present results from Cox proportional hazard modeling shown in Figure 6. The statistical approach is appropriate for time-to-event data. P-values and hazard ratios are reported with confidence intervals. The cumulative disadvantage model is supported by the data showing additive effects. However, the gender classification limitation (C99-C103) propagates uncertainty into these results.

results.result: No K99 awardees were from HBCUs, and only two K99 awardees activated R00 awards at HBCUs. In April 2023, there were limited active R01 awards at HBCUs: 8 at Morehouse School of Medicine, 9 at Howard, 5 at Meharry Medical College, and 5 at Jackson State University.
results.evaluation: Claims C11 and C126-C131 present stark findings about HBCU representation based on NIH Reporter data. The zero K99 awardees from HBCUs and two R00 activations at HBCUs are verifiable from the dataset. The R01 counts at specific HBCUs are point-in-time observations from April 2023 NIH Reporter queries.

results.result: Analysis of Wapman et al. faculty flow data (65,120 total flows) showed 296 faculty with doctoral degrees from HBCUs and 529 faculty at HBCUs. Howard University granted the most doctoral degrees leading to faculty appointments (116 individuals, with 56 staying at Howard). Florida A&M was second (44 total, 32 staying). Very few HBCU doctoral degree holders work at top-25 NIH-funded institutions. HBCU faculty ranks employ large numbers of faculty with HBCU doctoral degrees, with Howard showing more diversity in doctoral institution origins than other HBCUs.
results.evaluation: Claims C132-C142 analyze the publicly available Wapman et al. dataset, with clear methodology for field selection described in Methods. The faculty flow patterns are descriptive statistics from this dataset. Figure 7 provides visual support. The findings about HBCU self-hiring and limited representation at top-funded institutions are straightforward data summaries.

results.result: Self-hiring rates vary by institution: 25% at USC, 10-12% at Duke and Yale, and relatively few at Princeton. Certain institutions (Harvard, Columbia, Penn, Stanford, Johns Hopkins, Michigan, UC Berkeley, Duke, UNC) are nearly ubiquitous in top-15 doctoral degrees for faculty at many institutions. Regional hiring patterns exist (e.g., Tufts/BU common at Harvard, Wayne State at Michigan). Faculty at private top-funded institutions tend to have degrees from other well-funded private institutions, while public institutions show similar within-category hiring patterns. HBCU doctoral degree holders rarely exceed 2% of faculty except at other HBCUs.
results.evaluation: Claims C143-C156 present faculty hiring patterns from the Wapman et al. dataset, supported by Figure 7 supplements. The self-hiring rates and regional patterns are descriptive statistics. The observation about institutional prestige hierarchies aligns with prior literature (C157). The finding about HBCU doctoral holders being rare outside HBCUs is a straightforward data summary.

results.result: FOIA data from 2007-2017 showed successful K99 award rates of 31.0% for white applicants, 26.7% for Asian applicants, and 16.2% for Black applicants. R00 transition rates were 77% for white, 76.1% for Asian, and 60.0% for Black K99 awardees. While gender equity has improved, a significant racial equity gap persists.
results.evaluation: Claims C193-C197 cite specific FOIA data (request #47950) from Dr. Pickett for fiscal years 2007-2017. The racial disparities in both K99 award rates and R00 transition rates are clearly documented. The interpretation that racial equity gaps persist while gender equity has improved (C197) is supported by comparing these racial disparities with the gender parity in conversion rates (C101).

results.result: 755 extramural K99 awardees did not receive R00 awards. Of these, 426 received K99 awards in 2020 or later and may still be in the K99 phase, while 329 were from 2019 or earlier and are likely no longer eligible for R00 awards.
results.evaluation: Claims C54-C56 and C175 present straightforward counts from the NIH Reporter data about K99 awardees who did not transition to R00. The temporal cutoff reasoning (2019 or earlier being past eligibility) is logical given the 2-year K99 phase plus potential 1-year no-cost extension mentioned in the text. However, the manuscript acknowledges not knowing where these awardees went or why they didn't receive R00 awards.

results.result: In the beginning of the K99/R00 program, nearly all awardees staying at the same institution remained in the same department. From 2013 onward, a greater number moved to new departments within the same institution.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C70 describe temporal trends in departmental mobility for same-institution R00 activations, supported by Figure 1F. This represents a straightforward descriptive finding about changing patterns over time in the program.

results.result: K99 to R00 faculty flow generally follows prestige hierarchies with some institutional deviation. Prestige hierarchies in academic biomedical science align with NIH funding portfolio size, supporting a core-periphery structure of hiring.
results.evaluation: Claims C162-C163 synthesize the hiring flow patterns (C85-C91, C104-C112) with reference to Wapman et al.'s conceptual framework. The alignment of prestige with NIH funding is directly demonstrated by the data showing top-funded institutions producing and recruiting the most awardees. This represents a valid inference from the presented data.

results.result: Demonstrating independence from the postdoctoral advisor is a key component of R00 activation. Moving to a new institution clearly establishes independence, but staying at the same institution may result in disadvantages including reduced start-up packages, additional service duties, more committee work, or internal/reviewer bias about independence.
results.evaluation: Claim C164 states general knowledge about R00 requirements. Claim C165 makes a logical inference. However, claims C166-C169 are explicitly speculative explanations for the observed disadvantage (C113). The manuscript uses phrases like 'may be due to' and 'alternatively, this may be' indicating these are hypotheses rather than demonstrated mechanisms. No data are presented to test these specific explanations.

results.result: Cumulative disadvantages may contribute to lower likelihood of promotion/tenure and gender disparities in faculty ranks and leadership. Additional disadvantages may exist for transgender, gender non-binary, non-conforming individuals, those from systematically marginalized groups, or those with disabilities.
results.evaluation: Claims C171 and C173 are explicitly speculative inferences from the observed disadvantages (C113-C123). The manuscript uses 'may contribute' indicating these are hypotheses about downstream effects rather than demonstrated outcomes. No data on promotion, tenure, or leadership positions are presented. Claim C173 acknowledges unmeasured disadvantages beyond the binary gender classification used.

results.result: The concentration of K99 awards at top-funded institutions may be due to built-in grant writing support, greater access to scientific discoveries, or institutional prestige bias in grant review. The grant review system may have inherent bias toward less prestigious institutions.
results.evaluation: Claims C176-C178 and C180-C181 are explicitly speculative explanations for the observed concentration of K99 awards (C106-C107). The manuscript acknowledges that data on unfunded K99 applications are not publicly available (C174), preventing direct testing of these hypotheses. Claim C181 interprets the data as showing bias, but alternative explanations (e.g., differential application rates, applicant qualifications) are not ruled out.

results.result: Self-hiring within HBCUs may occur to enable institutional survival. The K99 MOSAIC program may increase equity, as might efforts to fund career development awards specifically at HBCUs.
results.evaluation: Claims C189, C191, and C192 are explicitly speculative. Claim C189 offers a hypothesis about HBCU self-hiring without supporting data. Claims C191-C192 suggest potential interventions but acknowledge the MOSAIC program is too new to evaluate (C29). These represent policy recommendations rather than demonstrated findings.

results.result: The study is limited to K99/R00 awardees and faculty flows within the United States, excluding scientists without K99/R00 awards. Public data lack demographic details including self-identified gender, race, ethnicity, age, and degree type.
results.evaluation: Claims C198-C200 accurately describe study limitations. These are straightforward statements about scope and data availability that are verifiable from the Methods section and NIH Reporter database structure.

results.result: The K99/R00 mechanism increases awardees' chances of securing faculty positions but doesn't guarantee them. Understanding these factors may help grant reviewers, hiring committees, and funding bodies more equitably evaluate candidates. Improvements could be achieved through NIH systemic changes or individual faculty searches, with systemic change likely more impactful.
results.evaluation: Claim C201 is a reasonable inference from the 78-89% conversion rate (C59-C60), though 'undoubtedly' overstates certainty. Claim C202 appropriately acknowledges limitations. Claims C203-C205 are recommendations for future action rather than demonstrated findings. The suggestion that 'systemic change will likely lead to more impactful change' (C205) is logical but not empirically tested in this study.

results.result: The authors report that approximately 230 K99 awards were made annually from 2006-2022, representing up to $250 million in annual investment. From 2008-2021, an average of 234 extramural K99 awards were made per year, and from 2009-2022, an average of 198 R00 awards per year.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly accept these descriptive statistics about the K99/R00 program. One reviewer notes the authors 'used publicly available data...to examine some of the academic characteristics' and describes the analysis as 'reasonable.' Another reviewer states the study 'examined publicly available data on the distribution of the National Institutes of Health's K99/R00 awards' without questioning these basic program statistics.

results.result: The authors report that about 40% of K99 awardees were women, approximately 89% of K99 awardees went on to receive R00 awards (81.8% on a rolling basis excluding 2006-2007), and men make up 58% of both K99 and R00 awardees. The same percentages of men and women K99 awardees convert their K99 awards to R00 awards, though men have received more K99 awards than women each year since 2006.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept these gender-related findings without challenge. One reviewer notes the authors 'analyze the data by gender' and describes the analysis as 'reasonable.' Another reviewer explicitly states 'the conclusions are well-supported by the data, and limitations of the data and the name-gender matching algorithm are described satisfactorily,' indicating acceptance of the gender classification methodology and findings.

results.result: The authors demonstrate that institutions with the most NIH funding produced and recruited the most K99/R00 awardees. K99 awards were granted to 256 institutions while R00 awardees represented 357 institutions. A small number of elite institutions (Stanford, UCSF, Massachusetts General Hospital) dominated K99 awards, with 54% of all K99 awardees at 10% of institutions. Awards were concentrated in East and West coast states, particularly California, Massachusetts, and New York.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly affirm these institutional concentration findings. One reviewer states the authors 'establish a clear overview of the institutional locations of K99 and R00 awardees' and notes 'there's a clear institutional hierarchy of hiring for K99/R00 researchers that echo previous research on the rigid faculty hiring networks.' Another reviewer describes the evidence as 'compelling evidence documenting the inequalities that shape faculty funding opportunities and career pathways.'

results.result: The authors report temporal trends in K99-to-R00 conversion rates and institutional mobility. Until 2015, conversion rates were similar for those staying versus moving institutions, but after 2015, the activation rate for those staying at the same institution decreased. The proportion staying at the same institution declined from ~30% in early years to ~20% from 2013 onward. Self-hiring rates vary by institution type, with 36% at private institutions with large NIH funding portfolios versus 18.5% at public institutions with smaller portfolios.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept these mobility findings without challenge. One reviewer notes 'the finding that researcher mobility has the largest effect on subsequent funding success is key and novel' and states 'other data supplement this finding: for example, although the total number of R00 awards has increased, most of this increase is for awards to individuals moving to different institutions. In 2010, 60% of R00 awards were activated at different institutions compared to 80% in 2022.'

results.result: The authors demonstrate that time to receive a major NIH award after starting an R00 ranged from 4.6 to 7.4 years, with significantly longer times for women, those who remained at their home institution, and those at institutions outside the top 25 NIH-funded. Cox proportional hazard analysis identified staying at the same institution as the greatest disadvantage (hazard ratio 0.7095, p<0.0001), followed by R00 institution funding level and gender. Each cumulative disadvantage increased median time by ~6 months and reduced overall chance by 5-6%.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly affirm these cumulative disadvantage findings as a major contribution. One reviewer states 'Men who moved to a top-25 NIH funded institution in their postdoc-to-faculty transition experienced the shortest median time to receiving a R01 award, 4.6 years, in contrast to the median 7.4 years for women working at less well-funded schools who remained at their postdoc institutions.' Another reviewer notes 'these results empirically demonstrate that even after receiving a prestigious early career grant, researchers with less mobility belonging to disadvantaged groups at less-resourced institutions continue to experience barriers.'

results.result: The authors report that there has yet to be a K99 awardee at a historically Black college or university (HBCU), and only two K99 awardees activated R00 awards at HBCUs out of 2,703 total K99-to-R00 transitions. The authors also document limited R01 funding at HBCUs (8 at Morehouse, 9 at Howard, 5 at Meharry, 5 at Jackson State as of April 2023).
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly highlight these HBCU findings as critically important. One reviewer states 'The authors also highlight two incredible facts: No postdoc at a historically Black college or university (HBCU) has been awarded a K99 since the program's launch. And out of all 2,847 R00 awards given thus far, only two have been made to faculty at HBCUs. Given the track record of HBCUs for improving diversity in STEM contexts, this distribution of awards is a massive oversight that demands attention.' Another reviewer notes 'documenting the pathways of HBCU faculty is an important extension of the study.'

results.result: The authors demonstrate institutional hiring patterns showing that most K99 awardees attain faculty positions at private institutions (62% vs 38% public), with 45% of K99 awards going to the top 25 highest funded institutions (only 24 institutions) versus 55% to 226 lower funded institutions. For R00 awards, the distribution was more even with 32% to top 25 institutions and 68% to 327 lower funded institutions. Private institutions with high NIH funding preferentially hire from other private institutions, while public institutions with smaller portfolios have hired 74% of K99 awardees from similar institutions.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept these institutional flow patterns without challenge. One reviewer notes the authors 'establish a clear overview of the institutional locations of K99 and R00 awardees and the pathways for K99-to-R00 researchers' and states 'there's a clear institutional hierarchy of hiring for K99/R00 researchers that echo previous research on the rigid faculty hiring networks across fields.' The analysis is described as providing 'compelling evidence documenting the inequalities that shape faculty funding opportunities and career pathways.'

results.result: Using the Wapman et al. dataset, the authors analyze faculty flows showing that 296 faculty members have doctoral degrees from HBCUs out of 65,120 total faculty flows, with 529 faculty at HBCUs. Howard University granted the most doctoral degrees (116) that led to faculty appointments, with the majority (56) working at Howard. HBCU doctoral degree holders are rare at non-HBCU institutions (not exceeding 2% except at Middle Tennessee State at 3.9%). Self-hiring is common at most institutions (10-20%), and HBCUs appear to be the only institution type that hires faculty with doctoral degrees from other HBCUs. The authors document regional and institutional prestige-based hiring patterns across all institution types.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly affirm the HBCU faculty flow analysis as an important contribution. One reviewer states 'documenting the pathways of HBCU faculty is an important extension of the study by Wapman et al. (2022), and provides a more nuanced look at the pathways of faculty beyond the oft-discussed high status institutions.' The analysis is accepted without methodological concerns, though one reviewer notes 'there is a need for more refinement in this segment of the analyses' without specifying what refinement is needed.

results.result: The authors conclude that K99 to R00 faculty flow generally follows similar hierarchies with some deviation for specific institutions, and that prestige hierarchies in academic biomedical science align with NIH funding portfolio size. They interpret their findings as consistent with the Matthew effect and the universal core-periphery structure of hiring described by Wapman et al.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly affirm these interpretive conclusions. One reviewer notes 'some of the observed funding and hiring traits are in line with the Matthew effect in science (Merton, 1968) and in science funding (Bol et al., 2018).' Another reviewer states the findings 'enhance previous work on the relationship between mobility and ones' access to resources, collaborators, or research objects' and that the results 'empirically demonstrate' the persistence of barriers even after receiving prestigious early career grants.

results.result: The authors report data from a 2018 FOIA request showing that for fiscal years 2007-2017, the successful K99 award rate for white applicants was 31.0%, compared to 26.7% for Asian applicants and 16.2% for Black applicants. R00 transition rates were also higher for white K99 applicants (77%) compared to Asian (76.1%) and Black (60.0%) awardees. The authors conclude that while improvements in equity between male and female applicants have occurred, there is still a significant racial equity gap.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly acknowledge these racial disparity findings. One reviewer states 'Although data on applications versus awards for the K99/R00 mechanism are limited, there exists data for applicant race and ethnicity for the 2007-2017 period, which were made available by a Freedom of Information Act request' and notes 'These results are highly relevant given the discussion of K99 award impacts on the sociodemographic composition of U.S. biomedical faculty.' The reviewer provides the specific numbers, indicating acceptance of the findings.

results.result: The authors speculate about various mechanisms that might explain their findings, including reduced start-up packages for internal candidates, additional service work burdens, bias in grant review, institutional support differences, and potential benefits of mobility. They suggest that the K99 MOSAIC program and targeted funding at HBCUs may increase equity, and that systemic change through NIH policy may be more impactful than individual faculty search improvements.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept these speculative interpretations and policy implications as reasonable. One reviewer notes 'The findings can provide further insights for the leadership at funding and hiring institutions and science policy makers for individual and large-scale improvements that can benefit the scientific community.' Another states 'This result has important policy implications aimed at reducing funding disparities - mainly that interventions that focus solely on early career or early stage investigator funding alone will not achieve the desired outcome of improving faculty diversity.'

results.result: The authors acknowledge several study limitations: focus on K99/R00 awardees only (excluding non-awardees), limitation to U.S. faculty flows, lack of demographic details in public data (self-identified gender, race, ethnicity, age, degree type), and unavailability of data on unfunded K99/R00 applications.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly acknowledge and accept these limitations. One reviewer states 'At no fault of the authors, the analysis is limited to only examining K99 awardees and not those who applied but did not receive the award. This limitation is solely due to the lack of data made publicly available by the NIH.' Another notes 'the limitations of the data are described adequately' and 'limitations of the data and the name-gender matching algorithm are described satisfactorily.'

comparisons.comparison: Perfect agreement. Both OpenEval and peer reviewers find the descriptive statistics about K99/R00 award numbers (C1, C2, C52, C57, C58) to be SUPPORTED. Both note these are straightforward data summaries from NIH Reporter without complex statistical analysis required.

Disagreement on gender classification methodology. OpenEval rates claims C3, C99-C103 as UNCERTAIN due to inherent biases in name-to-gender classification that cannot capture transgender, non-binary, or gender non-conforming individuals.
